ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

wrist — clinical pattern 1

A 24-year-old man falls onto an extended wrist. He has focal anatomical snuffbox tenderness and pain with scaphoid-tubercle palpation. Initial radiographs are unrevealing, but the clinician protects the wrist and arranges further assessment for an occult fracture. Which injury is suspected?

  1. Scapholunate ligament injury
  2. Triangular fibrocartilage complex injury
  3. Perilunate dislocation
  4. Lunate dislocation
  5. Scaphoid fracture
Answer and explanation

Scaphoid fracture

Focal snuffbox or scaphoid-tubercle tenderness after a fall raises concern for scaphoid fracture even when initial films are negative.

Option explanations

Scaphoid fracture: Focal snuffbox or scaphoid-tubercle tenderness after a fall raises concern for scaphoid fracture even when initial films are negative.

Scapholunate ligament injury: Scapholunate dissociation widens the interval between the scaphoid and lunate and can cause dorsal wrist pain or instability. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Triangular fibrocartilage complex injury: The TFCC supports the ulnar wrist and distal radioulnar joint; injury can produce ulnar-sided pain and pain with rotation. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Perilunate dislocation: The lunate remains aligned with the radius while the capitate and remaining carpus are displaced, commonly dorsally. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Lunate dislocation: The lunate itself displaces, typically volarly, losing its normal relationship with the distal radius and capitate. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
